summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application in full: DAO layer (sqli/dao/*), views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 setup, config, and templates. The application is riddled with deliberate, reachable vulnerabilities: an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create, globally disabled HTML autoescaping leading to stored XSS, CSRF protection commented out, unsalted MD5 password hashing, non-HttpOnly session cookies, and write endpoints with no authorization. Overall risk is critical: a remote unauthenticated attacker can inject SQL and persist XSS. Coverage is the entire Python source and templates; static JS/CSS assets and binary fonts were not analyzed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds its INSERT by Python %-formatting the caller-supplied name directly into the SQL string instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The students() view (sqli/views.py:54-57) calls Student.create(conn, data['name']) with the raw POST field on every POST to /students/, and that route has no authorization check and CSRF is disabled, so any remote unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary SQL. A name like ') ; DROP TABLE students;-- or a stacked/subquery payload executes against PostgreSQL, allowing data exfiltration (e.g. dumping users.pwd_hash), modification, or destruction.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> await cur.execute(q). Source: views.students -> data['name'] from await request.post(). Contrast with every other DAO method which uses parameterized execute(q, params).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL with %/format/f-strings.

findings.title: Stored XSS from Jinja2 autoescape disabled globally
findings.description: The Jinja2 environment is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables render unescaped unless an explicit |e filter is applied. User-controlled, persisted values are rendered raw: course review text (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22), student names (students.jinja2:16 and course.jinja2:49), and course title/description (courses.jinja2:17-18, course.jinja2:14-15). An attacker who submits a review, student, or course containing <script> stores XSS that executes in every visitor's browser (including admins). Combined with non-HttpOnly session cookies this yields session hijacking.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` fed by Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) from views.review -> data.get('review_text').
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping: setup_jinja(..., autoescape=True) (or select_autoescape). Keep explicit |safe only where output is known-trusted HTML.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: A working CSRF middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:26-38) and templates emit _csrf_token hidden fields, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware chain. As a result no POST endpoint validates the CSRF token. An attacker can forge cross-site requests that create students (triggering the SQL injection), create courses, post reviews, submit marks, or log a victim out, using the victim's authenticated session.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[ session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware ]. The csrf_middleware in middlewares.py compares session['_csrf_token'] to form field but is never registered.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middlewares list and ensure the session token is set/verified on all state-changing POST handlers.

findings.title: Unsalted MD5 used for password hashing and verification
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored pwd_hash to a bare, unsalted MD5 of the supplied password. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: if the users table is disclosed (e.g. via the SQL injection above), password hashes are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/GPU brute force, and identical passwords across users yield identical hashes. The comparison is also non-constant-time.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  (from hashlib import md5).
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password KDF such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 (e.g. passlib/argon2-cffi) and a constant-time verify; migrate stored hashes on next login.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS (autoescape disabled), an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, enabling full account/session takeover including admin sessions.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (defaults to True) and additionally set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing write endpoints
findings.description: The students() (POST /students/) and courses() (POST /courses/) handlers perform inserts without any authentication or authorization check — the @authorize decorator is only applied to logout. The UI merely hides the forms for non-admins, but the handlers accept any POST. Any unauthenticated remote user can create students (the SQL-injection sink) and courses. The review() and evaluate() handlers are likewise unauthenticated for writes. Reported once here as representative; the same missing guard applies to views.review (lines 111-131) and views.evaluate (lines 134-153).
findings.evidence: async def students(request): ... if request.method=='POST': await Student.create(conn, data['name'])  — no get_auth_user/authorize. async def courses(...) same pattern. Only logout uses @authorize().
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize()/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) (as appropriate) to all POST handlers that mutate data, matching the privilege the UI implies.
